report:
**Conclusion: yes—but not as a guarantee.** For people hospitalized with *severe or critical* COVID-19, systemic corticosteroids (“cortisone-like” anti-inflammatory drugs), particularly low-dose dexamethasone, improve average survival compared with usual care. They do not ensure that any individual patient will survive.

The strongest direct evidence is the large randomized RECOVERY trial. Dexamethasone 6 mg daily for up to 10 days reduced 28-day mortality among patients already receiving invasive mechanical ventilation or supplemental oxygen; it did **not** show benefit for patients needing no respiratory support. Random allocation is important: it makes differences in outcomes much more plausibly attributable to the drug rather than baseline illness differences.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2021436

Independent corroboration came from the WHO REACT prospective meta-analysis of seven randomized trials in critically ill patients. Across the trials, systemic corticosteroids versus placebo/usual care were associated with lower all-cause mortality at 28 days. This supports that the effect is not confined to one hospital system or to dexamethasone alone.  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2770279

Accordingly, WHO makes a **strong recommendation** for systemic corticosteroids in severe and critical COVID-19, while suggesting against them in non-severe disease. The distinction matters: steroids suppress harmful inflammation in advanced disease, but early use may suppress useful antiviral immune responses without offsetting benefit.  
https://www.who.int/docs/default-source/coronaviruse/module-3-corticosteroid-therapy-and-covid19.pdf

Treatment requires clinical supervision: corticosteroids can raise blood glucose and may carry other risks, so dose, timing, and monitoring matter.  
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9359482
